blocks.text: Nobody instructed the traders of Kano to stock more tomatoes last week, yet the tomatoes arrived. Nobody's private profit built the Third Mainland Bridge, yet it stands. Nigeria answers the same economic questions in two very different ways at once — and that is what makes it a mixed economy.

blocks.markdown: An **economic system** is the organised way a society uses its scarce resources to satisfy the wants of its members. No matter how rich or poor a country is, its system has to answer three basic questions.

items: **What to produce, and in what quantities?** Rice or tanks? Hospitals or football stadiums?
**How to produce it?** Labour-intensive hoes and cutlasses, or capital-intensive tractors?
**For whom to produce?** How is the output shared out among the population?

blocks.title: Price mechanism
blocks.text: The system by which the free movement of prices signals what consumers want, rations scarce goods among competing buyers, and rewards producers who supply what is in demand. It is sometimes called the invisible hand, after Adam Smith.

blocks.markdown:
### The three systems

Under **capitalism** (free enterprise) the means of production are privately owned, the profit motive drives decisions and the price mechanism answers all three questions.

Under **socialism** the state owns the major means of production, a central plan sets output targets, and the declared aim is equality rather than profit.

A **mixed economy** deliberately combines the two: private firms operate for profit alongside government ownership, regulation and public provision.

rows: The state on behalf of the people
Market, guided and supplemented by government

Conflict between the two sectors, heavy administration

blocks.caption: The three systems compared on ownership, motive and decision making

blocks.markdown:
### Why Nigeria is a mixed economy

Private Nigerians own farms, shops, transport fleets, banks and manufacturing plants, and they set their own prices and output. At the same time, the Federal and State Governments own and run refineries, universities, teaching hospitals, railways and the power transmission network, and they regulate the rest through bodies such as the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission.

Government has also moved back and forth between the two sectors. The Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decrees of 1972 and 1977 transferred businesses from foreign to Nigerian hands, while the privatisation programme that began under the Privatisation and Commercialisation Decree of 1988 and continued through the Bureau of Public Enterprises sold state assets, including the power distribution companies in 2013, back to private investors.

blocks.title: Deciding which system a description points to
blocks.prompt: A country's constitution vests ownership of all farmland and factories in the state; a National Planning Commission fixes annual output targets for cement and rice; wages are set by grade, and there are no privately owned companies. Which economic system is this, and give two likely consequences?

steps.text: Test ownership first. All land and factories belong to the state, so private ownership of the means of production is absent.
Test the allocation method. Output is fixed by a planning commission rather than by prices, so the price mechanism is not doing the allocating.
Test the motive. Wages are fixed by grade and there is no profit-seeking firm, so the motive is welfare and equality.
All three tests point to socialism, specifically a centrally planned economy.
Likely consequences: shortages and queues where planners underestimate demand, and weak incentives to innovate because no producer keeps the extra reward.

blocks.answer: A socialist (centrally planned) economy, with shortages and weak innovation incentives as typical consequences

blocks.title: Structure your comparison
blocks.text: When asked to compare economic systems, answer under fixed headings — ownership, motive, decision making, competition, income distribution. A tabulated or clearly headed answer earns full marks; a rambling paragraph rarely does.

points: Every economic system must answer what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom.
Capitalism relies on private ownership, the profit motive and the price mechanism.
Socialism relies on state ownership and central planning, aiming at equality.
A mixed economy combines private enterprise with public ownership and regulation.
Nigeria is a mixed economy: private business operates alongside government ownership, regulation and, since 1988, active privatisation.
